title: Chop wood, carry water
hook: Layman Pang's verse: the marvelous is in carrying water and chopping wood (Chan tradition)
carry: fully present to the weight of the bucket

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baizhang and the hidden tools. Your line was sleeves rolled up. Which chore did you take on? Today, another voice from the same Chan world, and it isn't a monk's. Day nine hundred.

What would count as a miracle in your house? A bill that pays itself? A teenager who empties the dishwasher unasked? In the Chan tradition, a man known as Layman Pang was asked by his teacher what his days had been like, and his answer, as it's handed down, is a short verse. Its punch line, in paraphrase: my supernatural power, my marvelous activity, is carrying water and hauling firewood. That's it. No flying. No reading minds. A bucket and a bundle of sticks. Today's word comes from that verse, in the shape people now pass it around: chop wood.
screen: `A MIRACLE IN YOUR HOUSE?` → `NO FLYING, NO MIND-READING.` → `A BUCKET AND SOME STICKS.`

segments.voice: First, who's speaking. Layman means he wasn't a monk. Chan tradition remembers Pang as a householder, with a family, who studied with Chan teachers and is remembered for sharp, plain answers. So the verse comes from someone living an ordinary life, not from behind monastery walls. Second, the turn in the verse. It opens by saying his daily affairs are nothing special, then reaches for some very big words, supernatural powers, marvelous functioning, and attaches them to the dullest jobs in the house. The joke is serious. Whatever is wonderful about awakening, the verse says, it shows up in the bucket and the firewood, not somewhere else. Third, the saying it turned into. You may have heard a version that goes: before enlightenment, chop wood, carry water; after enlightenment, chop wood, carry water. That neat line gets passed around, and it shares Layman Pang's spirit, but the words aren't his. His verse, as it's handed down, speaks of hauling firewood, not chopping it. Fourth, what changes if nothing changes. The chores stay the same. The water still has to be carried. What the verse points to is the one carrying it. A person can haul water while thinking of a hundred other places. Or a person can haul water. In Chan, that second way of doing it, fully present to the weight of the bucket, is not a step toward the practice. It is the practice.
screen: `A LAYMAN, NOT A MONK.` · `GRAND WORDS FOR DULL JOBS.` · `A SAYING, NOT HIS WORDS.` · `JUST CARRY THE WATER.` · then, large: `CHOP WOOD.`

segments.voice: Sit easily, and let the breath come and go. Choose one chore you'll do after the bell. Washing a pan. Folding a towel. Watering a plant. Then leave it there, and come back to this. Sitting is a chore too. Feel the weight of the body in the seat, the way a bucket pulls on the arm. Feel the breath carried in and carried out. When the mind leaves for a hundred other places, notice where it went, and pick the bucket back up. Let it be nothing special, and see whether that's the same as dull. If you pray, you can offer the chore in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Chop wood. From Layman Pang's Chan verse: the marvelous is found in carrying water and firewood, in the plain work of a day. Today's word.
Your line: fully present to the weight of the bucket. Today, do one chore as if it were marvelous, and let it be only that chore while you do it. Day nine hundred.

howItsDone: In Chan and Zen practice, daily chores such as cooking, cleaning and carrying are treated as part of meditation, and Layman Pang's verse is often quoted to make the point.

fork.setup: you're Layman Pang. your teacher asks what your days have been like. where do you say the marvelous is?
fork.reveal: his verse names carrying water and hauling firewood as his supernatural power and marvelous activity.

original.note: Chinese, from Layman Pang's verse: hauling firewood. the verse pairs it with carrying water.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm Zen poster about chores.
what it means: a Chan householder's verse that pins big spiritual words to carrying water and firewood.
what a scholar hears: Layman Pang's verse speaks of hauling firewood, not chopping it, and the before-and-after saying is a popular line, not his.

sources.ref: Chan tradition: the verse attributed to Layman Pang (Pang Yun), 'my supernatural power and marvelous activity: carrying water and hauling firewood'
sources.work: Chan Buddhist tradition (Recorded Sayings of Layman Pang)

notes: Layman Pang's verse paraphrased; Chinese commonly given as 神通并妙用，运水及搬柴. Confirm 搬柴 (ban chai, hauling firewood) and the claim that the verse says hauling, not chopping.
The 'before enlightenment, chop wood, carry water' saying is described as passed around with no clear source in the old texts. Confirm.
Pang described as a householder with a family who studied with Chan teachers: traditional account; confirm.
The script also says the verse opens with 'my daily affairs are nothing special'; confirm against the received text.
howItsDone says the verse is 'often quoted'; soften if a Keeper prefers.
